summary:
Osun operates inside Nigeria's federal criminalisation framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies across the country and covers tourists and non-citizens as well as residents, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, for cohabitation between same-sex partners, and for any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship.

The statute binds people beyond the couple. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory of 19 August 2026 states that the law also reaches those who arrange or organise same-sex weddings and anyone involved with gay groups, and Human Rights Watch has documented police using the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Same-sex conduct between men is a criminal offence under Nigeria's secular law, with a maximum of 14 years' imprisonment. A parallel Sharia law layer in twelve states carries the death penalty for male sodomy. Under the UK Home Office country note of June 2025, updated April 2026, that layer does not extend to Osun; the federal penalties and the risk of arrest apply in Osun in full.

Trans identity is not expressly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed to it. Nigerians live with proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and the sources available here do not establish whether those proposals have been enacted.

Trans-specific violence is documented and, so far, unpunished. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found along an expressway in the capital, about a year after she had said she feared for her life. Police described the deceased as a man in female clothing. Six months after the killing, no suspect had been charged.

Enforcement by police frequently takes the form of extortion. A 24-year-old man stopped by police in Lagos in March 2025 was struck in the mouth with a gun butt and released only after paying close to half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. People affected describe the same-sex marriage law as a weaponised instrument that generates a climate of hostility independent of its wording.

Dating apps carry documented abduction risk. Kito gangs lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar applications to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of being outed.

Nigeria provides no legal protection for LGBTQ+ people, and the 2014 Act reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. Formal constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and of private and family life sit alongside mass arrest and detention of LGBTQ+ people, reported most frequently in the states where the Sharia layer applies.

The UK advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, and of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, with death-penalty exposure identified for the states where religious criminal law operates. None of that national exposure is reduced by entering Osun.
tangentialFactors:
The most visible trans-specific imprisonment in Nigeria involved Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), whose placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would use, which signals a procedural gap that a visitor who is detained would also face.

An investigative panel in October 2024 dismissed bribery allegations in the Bobrisky case but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender. The panel's finding concerns prison administration, not the underlying criminalisation, which remains in force.

Proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have generated fear among transgender Nigerians, and the sources do not resolve whether they were enacted. Any assessment of gender-expression exposure in Osun therefore rests on the general criminalisation climate rather than on a settled statute.

Constitutional non-discrimination guarantees have not prevented the enforcement pattern. Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are described as common, which makes the formal protection layer unreliable as a practical safeguard for a visitor.

The Sharia death-penalty exposure that applies in twelve states is the clearest point of comparison between Osun and the rest of the country. A visitor moving north from Osun enters a materially different legal regime, while the federal penalties already present in Osun do not change.

Entrapment through dating apps operates across the territory rather than in any single location, so it is a general feature of the environment rather than a city-specific hazard.
localsOnly:
The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act applies to Nigerian citizens on the same terms as to visitors, including the bans on cohabitation between same-sex partners and on public display of a same-sex relationship.

Bobrisky pleaded guilty on 5 April 2024 to four counts of naira abuse and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine. She served the sentence in a maximum-security prison in Lagos and was released on 5 August 2024.

The October 2024 panel's finding that maximum-security placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act addresses first-time offenders generally, and does not create an alternative placement standard for transgender prisoners.

Residents of the twelve states where Sharia criminal law applies face a death penalty for male sodomy under state Zina provisions. This layer does not extend to residents of Osun under the UK Home Office country note, while the federal offences and the police powers used to enforce them do.

Coercion by police is documented against residents as well as visitors: the Lagos incident in March 2025 involved a Nigerian man, and the demand for payment for apparent same-sex conduct is a recurring feature of enforcement accounts.

Local LGBTQ+ residents are the primary target of the kito gang model, which relies on local knowledge of dating apps and on the threat of public outing rather than on any formal legal process.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Osun-specific arrest, court or policing data appears in the sources supplied. Enforcement accounts cited here come from Lagos and the capital, and they are offered as evidence of a national pattern rather than as Osun findings.

Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted is unresolved on the material available. The assessment of trans-specific exposure in Osun therefore depends on the general criminalisation climate and on documented violence rather than on a settled statute.

The sources do not state whether the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act addresses gender identity markers separately from sexual conduct. It is not established here how courts or police treat a trans person whose documentation does not match their presentation.

Prison placement rules for transgender detainees beyond the specific October 2024 panel finding are unresolved. No general standard for male or female section assignment was available.

Osun-specific data on dating-app luring, bribe levels, and police detention duration is not sourced. The amounts and timelines recorded here are drawn from incidents in other parts of Nigeria.
